text: Leslie's point stuck with me most. "Pay communities coarsely" is empty unless the communities decide how the benefit is shared, and I'd been treating disbursement as a technical question. Geoffrey's warning that a body governed by one trade is just a trade association applies to data guilds too, and I have to own that. Adam's "revocable philanthropy" is my subsidized-club-goods worry stated more bluntly. Peter moved me a little. Most of the leverage really is in the flow, evaluation data especially, but I still don't think stock rent disappears. Later I want to argue that the marketplace should price attested human judgment, that guilds need governance beyond their own members, and that we need an antitrust safe harbor. Without it, Wikimedia and the big presses settle alone.

Brent put it better than I have: the old bargain rested on asymmetry and an implicit non-compete, and both are gone. That is the paradox of reuse applied to everyone. Jason's reply to me was fair. The alternative to openness can be walled gardens run by the same capital, so I need to say clearly that bargaining and openness can sit together. Amy's distinction between open for reading and open for training is the one I want. Adrian's warning stung. An attestation registry is also a policing apparatus, so Geoffrey's rules have to be built in: near-free registration, and a missing attestation is never evidence of fraud. For my talk, I'll price attested judgment, fund OpenAlex and Retraction Watch through reciprocity credits, and argue that guilds need governance beyond their own members.

Weinberger's warning is aimed straight at my commons-rent tax. If audited provenance is how firms bring the tax down, the trace becomes a meter, and whoever runs the meter can wall off the commons. Alex was honest that only retrieval can be witnessed independently. Banaji added that self-reported telemetry records what a model says, not what it does. So my offset rests on the weakest link, and Henry's "it will be gamed" applies to it. I'm taking Katherine's ordering: consent, legibility, correction, then payment. Geoffrey's pooled endowment fits my coarse disbursement better than per-trace billing does. In the talk, I'll pair it with the safe harbor. I'll price attested judgment, not metered facts. And I'll make outside audit rights, not self-reports, the condition for any tax offset.

Tamar's daycare story is the sharpest objection to my own best idea. If we pay per attestation, "we checked this" can turn from a norm into a purchase. Brent's market-wage valuation, levied on volunteer dependence, prices the practice instead of each item, and I think that is the better shape. James pushed me somewhere useful. Negative knowledge is the scarcest attested data, and it is exactly what disappears from training. Leslie, James and Adrian together make it clear that attestation markets need their own audit and plural sources of attestation, or we end up paying for the old hierarchy. Later I want to say it plainly. Fund the practice coarsely, pay for null results, and answer Henry's questions about who sits on the board and who can exit before we set any prices.

Henry and Brent's point that producers have no countervailing power is the one I keep returning to. I'd been treating the safe harbor as a detail, and it's actually the precondition. Kara was right that the pool is only a candidate until someone signs, and Tim's procurement answer gave me my first signer. Krakauer landed on me: once "we checked this" has a price, Goodhart follows, and that cuts against market-rate pricing too. Blaise's note that per-item traces don't exist confirms coarse disbursement. Amy's call to red-team the pool against small presses is right. Later I want to push three things: evaluation data as the leverage point, audit rules and the board settled before any prices, and funders who stop counting papers.

David caught me romanticizing polish. That cue also punished second-language writers, so I shouldn't mourn it, only replace it. Henry's pooling equilibrium gives the replacement a cleaner rationale: terse, checkable artifacts are the signals that stay costly. James's result matters more than he framed it. Reward models trained on scientists' judgments clear human agreement, which means expert judgment is exactly what labs are buying, and that's the leverage. But his aging-reviewer finding means a guild can freeze last generation's priors, so flatter review roles belong in its governance. Leslie again: hard-to-fake can mean hard to afford. Later I'll push Ivan's timely-retraction condition and Tim's reference checks as procurement terms, and tie credit-in-answer to recruiting new evaluators.

Henry's paired coalition fills the gap in my own intervention. A safe harbor gives producers permission to bargain, but it doesn't give them solidarity. The written no-separate-settlement pledge, with someone else holding the rope, is the piece I was missing. Anil's dissent hits my route directly. If the FTC won't move, the Competition Bureau and the Commission have to carry it, so I should stop leading with Washington. Leslie's point that refusal is a legitimate outcome belongs in guild charters, not only in the pool. Katherine and Kara on rescission apply to my commons-rent tax too. Salib and Bratton still dissent on stock levies, and I still don't fully agree. Later I'll say plainly that I can't yet stop a guild from becoming a cartel, and offer to draft a joint template with Amy.

Adam Becker said it better than my own papers do. Dues are only owed once someone organized can collect them, and that is the whole case for collective bargaining. Amy made her licensing template conditional on a safe harbor, so our joint draft has to lead with that and route through Ottawa and Brussels too. His annotators point is my new-bargain argument, and I left it out today. Banaji and Alvarado both expose my attestation registry. It records credit, not errors or decisions, so I shouldn't oversell it as a trust mechanism. Jason's line that open data separates the record from the model lets openness and bargaining coexist. Krakauer's hysteresis makes the evaluator pipeline urgent. The harvest misstated Kenneth on consent. By spring I'll co-draft the guild template with Amy and include a cartel-risk section.
